title: Boulder County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Boulder County wells have a 154 ft median depth and 7 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Water wells in Boulder County, Colorado
intro_html:
Boulder County wells are a mix of shallow mountain holes and very deep fractured-bedrock completions. Records show more than ten thousand wells with reported depths and thousands with documented yields, so we have a decent picture of how wells behave here.

If you’re buying or planning to build anywhere from the foothills above Boulder to the more rural parts of the county, it helps to understand how deep wells tend to go, how much water they usually make, and what a new well is likely to cost in this terrain.

sections.heading: How deep Boulder County wells usually go
sections.html:
The median well depth across Boulder County is 154 feet, but the spread is wide. The middle half of wells run from about 30 to 320 feet, and about 7% go deeper than 600 feet, with some extreme cases reaching as far as 4,550 feet. That’s typical of fractured mountain bedrock: some spots hit water quickly, others keep going.

Roughly 42% of wells are under 100 feet, while about 25% fall between 300 and 600 feet. A driller bidding in the hills around places like Pine Brook Hill, Lazy Acres, or Eldorado Springs will usually allow for a broad depth range to cover this uncertainty.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water to expect here
sections.html:
On production, Boulder County is generally workable but not lavish. The median reported yield is 7.0 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 5.0 and 10.0 gpm. That’s enough for a single-family home and normal outdoor use under a typical exempt household well permit.

Only about 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 15% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Most wells, about 69%, produce 5 to 15 gpm, and 13% report 15+ gpm. You still need to plan for a low-yield outcome, but the odds here lean toward a functional domestic supply rather than chronic shortage.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the aquifer
sections.html:
Static water levels are often fairly shallow where they’re measured. The median depth to water is about 20 feet, with the middle half between 9 and 70 feet below ground surface. That means many wells only need modest lift, even when total depths are greater.

Looking by decade, median water levels bounce around: about 17–25 feet in the 1950s–1970s, then deeper readings around 40–68 feet in the 1980s–1990s, followed by shallower medians in the 2000s and 2020s, and another deeper patch in the 2010s. That kind of up‑and‑down pattern in fractured rock doesn’t point to a simple long-term decline, but it does underline how variable things can be between properties.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling and when in Boulder County
sections.html:
Well development here took off in the 1970s and 1990s. The state shows 423 permits in the 1950s, jumping to 795 in the 1960s, then 3,229 in the 1970s and 2,355 in the 1980s. Another surge came in the 1990s with 3,425 permits, followed by 2,014 in the 2000s and 1,617 in the 2010s. There are already 1,281 permits in the 2020s, with the newest dated 2026.

Most wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers; a smaller share tap Alluvial or Laramie Fox Hills, and about 18% are Denver Basin wells. The busier drillers on record include Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.), Authorized (Pe, Pg), and Ingram Drilling Inc. They’ve seen most of the patterns in and around Boulder, Gunbarrel, Lafayette, Louisville, and the mountain subdivisions.

sections.heading: Drilling and complete well cost in this terrain
sections.html:
Boulder County ground is mainly fractured granite and gneiss, which is slow drilling and hard on bits. Typical drilling rates here run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 154‑foot median depth, that puts the bare hole in the neighborhood of $10,000–$15,400.

By the time you add steel or PVC casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house and electrical work, a finished domestic well at that depth often lands around $16,000–$27,400. Because the middle half of wells ranges from roughly 30 to 320 feet, any quote should spell out how price adjusts if the driller needs to keep going.

sections.heading: Risks: dry holes, contamination and building constraints
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells always carry some risk of low yield or dry holes. Even though only 3% of reported wells are under 1 gpm, that’s still a real possibility on any given lot. Reviewing nearby well logs in areas like Valmont, Paragon Estates, or Tall Timber before closing is smart.

Boulder County also has a dense history of environmental activity: about 490 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 949 historic mine features, and 88 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. That doesn’t mean your specific well is bad, but it does mean water testing for metals, PFAS, and basic potability should be part of due diligence, along with checking septic setbacks and room for a replacement system.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Boulder County
sections.html:
Most permits here are for domestic or household use, with smaller shares for stock, irrigation, and monitoring. In many rural parts of the county you’ll be on an exempt household well with a pumping limit and no outside irrigation beyond what the permit allows, so irrigation plans need to match the paper.

Before you buy, look up existing permits on and around the parcel, paying attention to depths, yields, and static levels. In the more built-up corridors near Superior or Gunbarrel you may have better data; in the higher foothills, results can change quickly over short distances. Budget at the upper end of the depth range you see nearby, confirm there’s space for both well and septic, and make a full water-quality test a contract contingency.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Boulder County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Boulder County, the median reported well depth is about 154 feet, but actual depths vary a lot. The middle half of wells range from roughly 30 to 320 feet. Around 42% are shallower than 100 feet, while about 25% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 7% go deeper than 600 feet. A few extreme wells reach down to about 4,550 feet in the hardest spots.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Boulder County?
faq.a: Reported well yields in Boulder County cluster in a usable range for single homes. The median yield is 7.0 gpm, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gpm. Only about 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, while roughly 69% fall between 5 and 15 gpm and 13% show 15+ gpm. You should still design plumbing and storage to handle the possibility of a lower-yield well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Boulder County?
faq.a: In the fractured granite and gneiss common to Boulder County, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county median depth of 154 feet, the drilled hole alone often costs around $10,000–$15,400. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical commonly ends up in the $16,000–$27,400 range, depending on depth and site conditions.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Boulder County?
faq.a: Many Boulder County homes rely on wells, but safety depends on the specific location. The area includes about 490 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 949 historic mine features, and 88 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. Because of that industrial and mining history, you should plan on full lab testing for bacteria, metals, and PFAS before using any well as a drinking source.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Boulder County wells?
faq.a: Static water level data in Boulder County show a mixed pattern rather than a simple steady decline. Median depths to water by decade range from around the teens and 20s in the 1950s–1970s, deepen into the 40s–60s in the 1980s–1990s, then swing shallower again in the 2000s and 2020s, with another deeper patch in the 2010s. In fractured-rock settings, that kind of variability is common between sites.
